common_name: Flame Thrower Coleus (Bright Orange-Red Sun Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Flame Thrower holds its intense orange-red color well in more sun than many coleus cultivars, though afternoon shade helps prevent scorching in peak zone 9 summer heat.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun with some afternoon shade in the hottest climates. Flame Thrower produces broad leaves in blazing shades of orange and red radiating out from a darker center, giving the foliage a licking-flame pattern that intensifies with more sun exposure, similar in effect to Campfire but with a bolder, more variegated color break between zones. Pinch growing tips regularly to encourage bushy, well-branched growth and to remove flower spikes, which divert energy from foliage color and can cause the plant to decline after setting seed. Water regularly to keep soil evenly moist, and take stem cuttings in late summer to overwinter indoors as a houseplant, since coleus has no frost tolerance.

common_name: Gold Capella Schefflera (Bright Yellow-Variegated Dwarf Umbrella Tree)

planting.note: Plant outdoors after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March-May and bring containers indoors before temperatures drop below 35°F in fall. Remove any all-green reversion shoots immediately to prevent them from overtaking the variegated growth.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light to partial shade in well-drained, humus-rich potting mix or garden soil. Gold Capella carries even bolder, brighter golden-yellow variegation than the widely grown Trinette cultivar, with each glossy, umbrella-shaped leaflet splashed generously in yellow over a green base, giving the whole plant a sunnier, more luminous overall look useful for brightening a shaded corner. In zone 10-11 it can remain outdoors year-round as a landscape shrub; in zone 9 it is best managed as a container specimen moved outdoors for the warm season and overwintered indoors in a bright window. Prune leggy stems in spring to maintain a bushy, compact form, since schefflera responds well to hard pruning.

common_name: Frosty Pink Brugmansia (Double Pink Angel's Trumpet)

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; all parts of Brugmansia are toxic if ingested — plant away from children's play areas and wash hands after pruning.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade, keeping the root zone consistently moist through the growing season. Frosty Pink bears large, pendulous, double or semi-double trumpet flowers that open pale pink and fade toward a frosty white-pink at the ruffled, layered petal edges, a fuller, more complex bloom form than the simple single trumpets of many brugmansia cultivars, with the same heavy, sweet fragrance that intensifies in the evening. Like other brugmansia it is a fast, vigorous grower that benefits from regular feeding and consistent moisture to support its large leaves and near-continuous bloom in warm weather. Where winters bring hard freezes, cut back and mulch heavily or move container plants to a protected space, since brugmansia has no cold tolerance; all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.
sources: American Brugmansia and Datura Society reference

common_name: Jamaica Yellow Brugmansia (Vivid Golden Angel's Trumpet)

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; all parts of Brugmansia are toxic if ingested — plant away from children's play areas and wash hands after pruning.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade, keeping the root zone consistently moist through the growing season. Jamaica Yellow produces large, single, pendulous trumpet flowers in a vivid, saturated golden-yellow, deeper and warmer in tone than the softer butter-yellow of some other yellow brugmansia cultivars, carrying the same heavy, sweet evening fragrance typical of the genus. As with other brugmansia, it is a fast, vigorous grower that responds well to regular feeding and consistent moisture, rewarding good care with near-continuous bloom through the warm season. Where winters bring hard freezes, cut back and mulch heavily or move container plants to a protected space, since brugmansia has no cold tolerance; all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.
sources: American Brugmansia and Datura Society reference

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade, keeping the root zone consistently moist through the growing season. Pink Beauty produces large, single, pendulous trumpet flowers in a soft, clear pink that pales toward the throat, a gentler, more pastel display than the bolder magenta or fuchsia tones of some other pink brugmansia cultivars, carrying the same heavy, sweet fragrance that intensifies in the evening. Like other brugmansia it is a fast, vigorous grower that benefits from regular feeding and consistent moisture to fuel its large leaves and near-continuous warm-season bloom. Where winters bring hard freezes, cut back and mulch heavily or move container plants to a protected space, since brugmansia has no cold tolerance; all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

common_name: Bella Abutilon (Compact Seed-Grown Flowering Maple Series)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost, or plant nursery transplants after last frost into fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Bella is a compact, seed-grown series that blooms much sooner from seed than most abutilon cultivars, which are typically propagated only by cuttings.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade. Bella is a compact, mounding abutilon series bred to flower reliably from seed in a single season, unlike most flowering maple cultivars that must be grown from cuttings, producing an abundance of upward-facing, bell-shaped flowers in shades of red, orange, pink, yellow, and white over maple-shaped green leaves on a plant far shorter than the tall, leggy species types. Its small scale suits containers, hanging baskets, and the front of a mixed border where taller abutilon would be out of proportion. Pinch young plants to encourage bushier branching, and where winters bring hard freezes, grow it as a warm-season annual or bring a potted specimen indoors before frost.
